name: Refrigerator (full-size, ENERGY STAR)
note: ~510 kWh/yr, between ENERGY STAR model medians (362 top-freezer, 553 bottom, 640 side-by-side); compressor cycles

name: Refrigerator (older full-size, 1990s–early 2000s)
note: ~900 kWh/yr (ENERGY STAR: 2000 model 810, 1990 model 1,180 kWh/yr); compressor cycles

name: Mini fridge (compact, 1.7–4.5 cu ft)
note: ~250 kWh/yr (ENERGY STAR compact median 246; middle 80% 206–329); compressor cycles

name: Chest freezer (7–15 cu ft)
note: ~255 kWh/yr (ENERGY STAR chest models: 201–218 at 9–10.6 cu ft, 277 at 15.7 cu ft); compressor cycles

name: Upright freezer (frost-free, 13–20 cu ft)
note: ~438 kWh/yr (ENERGY STAR upright-freezer median); compressor cycles

name: Microwave (1,000 W cooking power)
note: Draws ~1.5x its cooking power from the outlet; 15 min/day of use

name: Drip coffee maker (10–12 cup)
note: Brewing one full pot (~15 min at full power); warming-plate time not included

name: Electric kettle (1.7 L)
note: About 12 min/day at full power (1–2 full boils)

name: Toaster (2–4 slice)
note: About 6 min/day (2–3 toasting cycles)

name: Induction burner (single, portable)
note: Medium-high setting, 1 h/day of cooking; the max setting draws up to 1,800 W

name: Slow cooker (6 qt)
note: One 8 h cook; Low is near the bottom of the range, High near the top

name: Electric pressure cooker (6 qt, Instant Pot type)
note: Full power until pressurized, then heater cycles; ~40% average over a 1 h cook (3 qt 700 W, 8 qt 1,200 W)

name: Blender (countertop)
note: Ordinary 350–450 W blender, 3 min/day; high-power blenders reach ~1,000 W

name: Rice cooker (5.5–6 cup)
note: ~30 min at full heat per batch (conservative); keep-warm not included. 3-cup 300 W, 10-cup up to 1,000 W

name: Box fan (20-inch)
note: Medium-high speed for 8 h

name: Ceiling fan (no light kit)
note: High speed for 8 h; ENERGY STAR 52-in. fans median ~26 W, older fans up to ~75 W

name: Window AC (5,000 BTU)
note: ~50% compressor duty on a hot day, 8 h/day (e.g., overnight); inverter ENERGY STAR units draw ~350 W

name: Window AC (8,000 BTU)
note: ~50% compressor duty on a hot day, 8 h/day; 8,000 BTU/h ÷ CEER 10.9–15 gives 530–735 W

name: Space heater (portable, 1,500 W)
note: High setting; thermostat assumed to run it ~50% of the time; 8 h/day

name: Electric blanket (full/queen)
note: Controller assumed ~50% duty at a medium setting; 8 h night. Single-size blankets ~60 W

name: Dehumidifier (50-pint)
note: Running W from ENERGY STAR capacity/IEF; humidistat assumed ~50% duty in a damp space

name: Gas furnace blower fan
note: ~50% run time in cold weather. Hardwired: needs a transfer switch or inlet to connect

name: CPAP (no humidifier)
note: 8 h night without humidifier or heated tube; many newer machines draw less

name: CPAP with heated humidifier
note: 8 h night with heated humidifier; ResMed power supplies are 65 W (AirSense 11) and 90 W (AirSense 10)

name: Portable oxygen concentrator (on AC)
note: Running and charging from its AC adapter; WHO puts portable units at 40–130 W, and Inogen One G5 / Philips SimplyGo adapters top out at about 120–150 W

name: Oxygen concentrator (home, 5 L/min)
note: Runs nonstop; 5 L/min home units are rated 275–400 W. Startup set at 1,200 W (3× the highest 5 L/min draw), per WHO’s 2–3× guidance, since makers don’t publish it

name: Wi-Fi router + modem
note: Modem plus Wi-Fi router left on 24 h

name: Phone charging (USB)
note: About one full smartphone charge per day (~2 h at ~10 W)

name: Laptop
note: Typical use for 6 h/day via its AC adapter

name: LED light bulb (60 W equivalent)
note: One 800-lumen LED bulb for 6 h/day

name: Starlink Standard
note: Starlink spec: 75–100 W average; on 24 h

name: Starlink Mini
note: Starlink spec: 25–40 W average; runs on 12–48 V DC or 100 W USB-C PD; on 24 h

name: Sump pump (1/3 HP)
note: Float switch cycles; assumes ~20% run time (12 min/hr) in wet weather; varies widely with inflow

name: Sump pump (1/2 HP)
note: Float switch cycles; assumes ~20% run time (12 min/hr) in wet weather; varies widely with inflow

name: Well pump (1/2 HP submersible)
note: ~1 h of pumping/day on pressure switch. Starting figure is Franklin's locked-rotor current for a 3-wire 230 V motor (23 A); 2-wire motors need more. Most 1/2 HP submersibles are 240 V; 120 V models exist

name: TV (55-inch LED)
note: Default picture settings, 4 h/day; ENERGY STAR 55-in. models measure 77–114 W

name: Desktop PC + monitor
note: Home/office PC (~120 W) plus LCD monitor (~30 W), 6 h/day; gaming PCs can reach 400 W

name: Game console (PS5 / Xbox Series X class)
note: Gameplay, 3 h/day; Sony measures ~215 W for PS5 games, ~90–115 W for PS4 games

name: Projector (home/portable)
note: 3 h/day (a movie or two); lamp-based home projectors sit at the high end

name: Washing machine
note: One ~1 h cold-water load; draw varies by cycle phase; water heating not included

name: Garage door opener
note: ~12 open/close runs of ~15 s each per day; standby draw not included

name: Circular saw (7-1/4 in.)
note: 30 min of cutting per day

name: Cordless tool battery charger
note: Standard 18/20 V charger, ~2 h/day (about two 5 Ah packs)

name: Pellet grill
note: ~300 W igniter phase at startup (535 W on some models), then ~50 W for auger/fan/controller; 4 h cook

name: E-bike charger (48 V, 2 A)
note: ~6 h refills a ~624 Wh battery, including charger losses

name: Aquarium heater (100 W)
note: Thermostat assumed ~50% duty; runs more in a cold room

name: 12 V compressor car fridge (DC)
note: Runs on 12 V DC; ~1.5 A average (Engel cites ~1–2 A typical); on 24 h

name: EV Level 1 charging (120 V, 12 A)
note: 12 A continuous at 120 V; ~5 mi of range per hour (AFDC), so 4 h/day adds ~20 mi
